text_blocks.snippet: Early symptoms of type 2 diabetes often develop slowly over several years and may be mild enough to go unnoticed. Many people have no symptoms at all during the early stages.
snippet_highlighted_words: often develop slowly over several years and may be mild enough to go unnoticed

list.snippet: Frequent Urination (Polyuria): Your kidneys work overtime to filter and flush out excess blood sugar, causing you to pee more often, especially at night.
Increased Thirst (Polydipsia): Fluid loss from frequent urination leads to constant thirst and a dry mouth.
Fatigue and Weakness: Because your cells cannot properly absorb glucose for energy, you may feel unusually tired, drained, or experience brain fog.
Blurred Vision: High blood sugar levels can cause fluid to shift and change the shape of the lenses in your eyes, making it hard to focus.
Increased Hunger (Polyphagia): Your body struggles to convert food into usable cellular energy, leaving you hungry shortly after eating.
Slow-Healing Sores or Cuts: Elevated blood sugar impairs circulation and weakens your immune response, causing minor wounds or cuts to take a long time to heal.
Tingling or Numbness: Peripheral nerve damage (neuropathy) can cause a pins-and-needles sensation, numbness, or burning in your hands or feet.
Darkened Skin Patches (Acanthosis Nigricans): Velvety, dark patches of skin—frequently on the neck, armpits, or groin—can be a visible sign of insulin resistance.
Frequent Infections: Higher blood sugar levels create an environment where bacteria and yeast thrive, leading to recurring urinary tract infections (UTIs) or yeast infections.
Unexplained Weight Changes: Some people experience unexpected weight loss as the body starts burning fat and muscle for fuel, while others may gradually gain weight.

text_blocks.snippet: For detailed clinical guidance and overview information, you can review resources from the Mayo Clinic and WebMD. A definitive diagnosis requires a simple blood test—such as a fasting blood glucose or A1C test—administered by a healthcare provider.
